lines: A scientist carries glowing test tubes around in her pocket.
Her name is Marie Curie.
In 1898, in Paris, she and her husband Pierre grind up a dark rock called pitchblende.
They hunt for something hidden inside.
It takes tonnes of rock.
From one tonne, they get just one tenth of a gram.
They name it radium, from the Latin word for ray.
Marie even invents the word radioactivity.
She stores the tubes in her desk drawer.
She loves the faint light they give off in the dark.
Nobody yet knows how harmful the rays are.
She works with no safety rules.
Her papers from the 1890s become radioactive too.
You see, it's like smoke soaking into your coat. Long after the fire is out, you still smell it.
Radium takes about one thousand six hundred years to lose half its strength.
So her notebooks will stay radioactive for well over a thousand years.
Today they sit in lead-lined boxes.
Anyone who wants to read them must wear protective clothing.
Even her cookbooks are highly radioactive.
In 1934, Marie dies at sixty-six, likely from the radiation.
Sixty years later, her remains are moved to the Panthéon in Paris.
They are sealed in lead, just like her notebooks.

claims.claim: Curie carried test tubes containing radioactive isotopes in her pocket and stored them in her desk drawer, remarking on the faint light they gave off in the dark.
In 1898 the Curies ground a sample of pitchblende; they eventually had to process tonnes of the ore, and from a tonne of pitchblende one-tenth of a gram of radium chloride was separated.
They named radium from the Latin word for 'ray' and coined the word 'radioactivity'.
The damaging effects of ionising radiation were not known at the time; her work was carried out without later safety measures.
Her papers from the 1890s are too radioactive to handle; even her cookbooks are highly radioactive; they are kept in lead-lined boxes and those who consult them must wear protective clothing.
Because radium-226 has a half-life of about 1,600 years, her notebooks are expected to remain radioactive for well over a thousand years.
Curie died in 1934, aged 66, of aplastic anaemia likely from exposure to radiation.
Sixty years later, in 1995, her remains were transferred to the Paris Panthéon and sealed in a lead lining because of the radioactivity.
